messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 45
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Chef
- Trauma Type: Rape
- Pcl5: 70

He is a 45-year-old Oceania man who has spent most of his adult life in kitchens, moving from one restaurant to another, learning how to keep calm when tickets pile up and the heat rises around him. Before the assault, he describes himself as the kind of chef who could handle anything if he stayed busy enough. He was divorced by then, living alone, and he had come to rely on work as the place where he felt most competent and least likely to be judged.

The assault happens after a late shift, when he agrees to have a drink with someone he knows from the restaurant scene. He remembers the evening in fragments at first: the noise of the bar, the pressure of being polite, the moment he realizes his body has gone cold and heavy instead of alert. What follows is not something he can fully arrange into a smooth story, even after telling it many times. He remembers fighting, then freezing. He remembers the shame more sharply than some of the physical details. What stays with him most is the sense that something in him leaves his body and watches from a distance while it happens, unable to stop it. In the days afterward, he moves through his apartment like a man carrying a concealed injury, showering repeatedly, changing clothes, scrubbing his skin until it is red, as if he can erase what happened by making himself cleaner.

At work, he returns too quickly because he does not know what else to do. The kitchen is loud, sharp, and structured, and for a while the routine helps. He can still dice onions, call orders, and time sauces by instinct. But he begins to notice that certain smells seize him without warning. A particular cologne on a customer, stale beer, the heat of a closed room after service—all of it can make his chest tighten and his thoughts race back to that night. He becomes hyperaware of exits, locks, and who is behind him. If someone approaches from the side unexpectedly, he jerks. He grows irritable with staff, snapping at small mistakes, then feeling ashamed and retreating into silence. He starts taking longer smoke breaks outside the back door just to breathe and check that nothing is about to happen to him.

Sleep becomes difficult. He falls asleep exhausted and wakes in the dark with his heart pounding, the assault returning in vivid pieces that feel less like memory than re-experience. Some nights he does not sleep at all. He lies on the couch with the television on for company, then notices dawn and realizes he has spent hours staring without taking anything in. When he does sleep, he wakes sweating, disoriented, and angry at his own body for producing a response he cannot control. He stops dating. Intimacy feels impossible; even casual touch can send a shock through him. He tells himself he is not interested, that he has too much work, too much stress, but underneath is a deep conviction that he is no longer safe with anyone and that something in him has been damaged beyond repair.

Over time, his world narrows. He drinks more often after shifts, not enough to pass out, but enough to blur the edges of memory. He avoids places that remind him of the assault, then later avoids places he once enjoyed because he cannot predict what will trigger him. He keeps his apartment dim and ordered, as if control over the environment might keep the past from breaking in. He feels detached from others, even from people he has known for years. When friends ask how he is, he gives practical answers about work and the restaurant, because speaking about feelings seems dangerous and humiliating. At times he thinks about what happened and feels disgust toward himself, as though his body’s reaction somehow made the assault his fault. At other times he feels numb, and the numbness is almost as frightening as the panic because it makes him wonder whether he is still himself.

Now, several sessions into telling his story, he still comes in guarded, with his arms crossed and his shoulders tense, but there are moments when his voice softens and he can say more than he thought possible. He is trying to understand why he feels as if he is always bracing for impact, why a hand on his shoulder can make him flinch, why he can be standing in a bright, busy kitchen and suddenly feel back in that room, trapped and powerless. He describes living with the sense that the assault did not end when it was over; instead, it continues to arrive in his body, in his sleep, in the split second before he trusts anyone, and in the way he keeps measuring every room for danger.
